```{r q15, fig.align = "center",fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = " Restaurant Lifespan Distribution"}
# If your industry labels vary (e.g., "Cafes" vs "Restaurant"),
# make a simple, robust harmonised label:
df_one_row <- df_one_row %>%
  mutate(
    industry_simple = case_when(
      str_detect(str_to_lower(industry), "takeaway") ~ "Takeaway",
      str_detect(str_to_lower(industry), "cafe|restaurant") ~ "Restaurant",
      TRUE ~ industry
    )
  )


#  Reusable plot function (same bins & colours as Shiny)

make_lifespan_hist <- function(data, title = "Lifespan Distribution") {
  plot_data <- data %>%
    mutate(
      lifespan_bin = if_else(lifespan_years >= 20, "20+", as.character(lifespan_years)),
      duration_grp = case_when(
        lifespan_years <= 2 ~ "Short-term (1–2 years)",
        lifespan_years <= 5 ~ "Medium-term (3–5 years)",
        TRUE               ~ "Long-term (6+ years)"
      )
    ) %>%
    count(lifespan_bin, duration_grp, name = "n") %>%
    mutate(
      lifespan_num = if_else(lifespan_bin == "20+", 20, as.numeric(lifespan_bin))
    ) %>%
    arrange(lifespan_num)

  ggplot(
    plot_data,
    aes(
      x = factor(lifespan_bin, levels = unique(lifespan_bin[order(lifespan_num)])),
      y = n,
      fill = factor(duration_grp,
                    levels = c("Short-term (1–2 years)",
                               "Medium-term (3–5 years)",
                               "Long-term (6+ years)"))
    )
  ) +
    geom_col(alpha = 0.8) +
    scale_fill_manual(
      values = c("Short-term (1–2 years)" = "#1f77b4",
                 "Medium-term (3–5 years)" = "#ff7f0e",
                 "Long-term (6+ years)"    = "#2ca02c"),
      name = "Duration"
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Lifespan (Years)",
      y = "Number of Businesses"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "right",
      axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
    )
}


# Build the two requested plots (Restaurant & Takeaway)

df_rest <- df_one_row %>% filter(industry_simple == "Restaurant")
df_take <- df_one_row %>% filter(industry_simple == "Takeaway")

p_restaurant <- make_lifespan_hist(df_rest,  "")
p_takeaway   <- make_lifespan_hist(df_take,  "")

# Print (or ggsave) as needed
```

Form (Figure \@ref(fig:q17) ), we observe dramatic geographic variations in business lifecycle patterns:

*High Early-Stage Failure Areas

Docklands: Shows the highest proportional concentration in 1-2 year band (~50% of all businesses)

Melbourne CBD: Despite 600+ total businesses, maintains a similar proportional pattern of early failures

West Melbourne (Residential): Shows heavy early-stage concentration

*Balanced Distribution Areas:


Carlton: Most balanced distribution across all lifecycle stages with ~90 businesses

North Melbourne & Kensington: Healthy representation across stages, suggesting sustainable market conditions

East Melbourne: Despite smaller numbers (~20), shows good lifecycle balance

*Limited Data Areas:

Port Melbourne, South Yarra, West Melbourne (Industrial): Too few businesses (≤4) for meaningful pattern analysis



Overall, areas with 40-150 total businesses (Carlton, North Melbourne, Southbank) show the most balanced lifecycle distributions, suggesting an optimal market size that avoids the hypercompetition seen in CBD while maintaining sufficient market depth.

Traffic density peaks overwhelmingly in Melbourne (CBD/Hoddle Grid). The hottest nodes align with Flinders St–Swanston St–Collins St corridors and around Flinders St Station/Bourke St Mall. This concentration is expected: the CBD combines (i) the city’s largest multimodal interchange (rail + tram), (ii) the highest daytime worker population, (iii) major retail anchors and visitor draws (laneways, malls, events), and (iv) short, walkable blocks that intensify pedestrian flow.

Spillover intensity is next strongest in Southbank (arts precinct, riverside promenade, Crown/Convention Centre) and parts of the east-end CBD; it drops sharply toward Docklands, West Melbourne, and the northern fringe, reflecting fewer transit nodes, wider blocks, and more office/residential land uses with lower all-day pedestrian churn.

Viable “busy-street” opportunities are highly localized—micro-site accuracy inside the CBD (and Southbank) matters far more than choosing a broad suburb label.



```{r include=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(cluster) 
library(factoextra) 

library(ggdendro)
# Load data
df_full <- read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv")

# Bias-free cohort (closed OR veteran) AND valid start (first_seen > 2002 OR veteran)
df_analysis <- df_full %>%
   filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE, start_year_filter == TRUE) %>%    # ← add this condition
  arrange(business_id, census_year) %>%
  group_by(business_id) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%   # first observation per business
  ungroup()



# CLUE AREA CLUSTERING



# Aggregate metrics by area
area_metrics <- df_analysis %>%
  group_by(clue_area) %>%
  summarise(
    # Sample size
    n_businesses = n(),
    
    # Survival metrics
    mean_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years),
    median_lifespan = median(lifespan_years),
    success_rate = mean(lifespan_group == ">12 yrs") * 100,
    
    # Competition metrics
    mean_same_ind = mean(same_industry_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_other_ind = mean(other_industry_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_total_comp = mean(competitors_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Business characteristics
    mean_seats = mean(num_seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_cafe = mean(industry == "Cafes") * 100,
    pct_outdoor = mean(str_detect(seating_type, "Outdoor")) * 100,
    
    # Variability
    sd_lifespan = sd(lifespan_years),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_businesses >= 20)  # Only areas with sufficient data



# Prepare clustering features (standardized)
area_features <- area_metrics %>%
  dplyr::select(
    mean_lifespan,
    success_rate,
    mean_total_comp,
    mean_seats,
    sd_lifespan
  ) %>%
  scale() %>%
  as.data.frame()

rownames(area_features) <- area_metrics$clue_area


# Determine optimal number of clusters




# Elbow method
set.seed(42)
wss <- sapply(2:8, function(k) {
  kmeans(area_features, centers = k, nstart = 25)$tot.withinss
})

# Silhouette method
sil_widths <- sapply(2:8, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(area_features, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  ss <- silhouette(km$cluster, dist(area_features))
  mean(ss[, 3])
})

# Find optimal
optimal_k <- which.max(sil_widths) + 1
cat("Optimal clusters (silhouette method):", optimal_k, "\n\n")

# Create elbow + silhouette plots
p_elbow <- data.frame(k = 2:8, wss = wss) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = k, y = wss)) +
  geom_line(color = "#3498db", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#3498db", size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = optimal_k, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Elbow Method", x = "Number of Clusters", y = "Within-cluster SS") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

p_silhouette <- data.frame(k = 2:8, silhouette = sil_widths) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = k, y = silhouette)) +
  geom_line(color = "#2ecc71", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#2ecc71", size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = optimal_k, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(title = "Silhouette Analysis", x = "Number of Clusters", 
       y = "Average Silhouette Width") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

# Perform clustering




set.seed(42)
km_areas <- kmeans(area_features, centers = optimal_k, nstart = 50)

# Add cluster assignments
area_metrics$cluster <- km_areas$cluster

# Order clusters by performance (best = 1, worst = highest number)
cluster_performance <- area_metrics %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(avg_success = mean(success_rate), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_success)) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number())

area_metrics <- area_metrics %>%
  left_join(cluster_performance %>% dplyr::select(cluster, rank), by = "cluster") %>%
  mutate(cluster_ordered = rank) %>%
  dplyr::select(-rank)

# Assign tier names
tier_names <- c("Tier 1: Prime Locations", "Tier 2: Solid Locations", 
                "Tier 3: Moderate Locations", "Tier 4: Challenging Locations")
tier_names <- tier_names[1:optimal_k]

area_metrics <- area_metrics %>%
  mutate(tier = tier_names[cluster_ordered])

# Cluster Profiles


cluster_summary <- area_metrics %>%
  group_by(tier, cluster_ordered) %>%
  summarise(
    n_areas = n(),
    n_businesses = sum(n_businesses),
    avg_lifespan = round(mean(mean_lifespan), 1),
    avg_success_rate = round(mean(success_rate), 1),
    avg_competition = round(mean(mean_total_comp), 0),
    areas = paste(clue_area, collapse = ", "),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(cluster_ordered)

#print(cluster_summary)






# Visualizations


# PCA for 2D visualization
pca_result <- prcomp(area_features)
pca_data <- as.data.frame(pca_result$x[, 1:2])
pca_data$cluster <- factor(area_metrics$cluster_ordered)
pca_data$tier <- area_metrics$tier
pca_data$area <- area_metrics$clue_area
pca_data$success_rate <- area_metrics$success_rate

var_explained <- summary(pca_result)$importance[2, 1:2] * 100

p_pca <- ggplot(pca_data, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = tier, size = success_rate)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = area), size = 2.5, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, 
            nudge_x = 0.1, nudge_y = 0.1, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(3, 10)) +
  labs(
    title = "CLUE Area Clustering (PCA Visualization)",
    subtitle = "Size = Success Rate | Color = Performance Tier",
    x = paste0("PC1 (", round(var_explained[1], 1), "% variance)"),
    y = paste0("PC2 (", round(var_explained[2], 1), "% variance)"),
    color = "Tier",
    size = "Success Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "right")

# Hierarchical clustering dendrogram
dist_matrix <- dist(area_features)
hc <- hclust(dist_matrix, method = "ward.D2")

dend_data <- dendro_data(hc)
dend_data$labels$label <- area_metrics$clue_area[as.numeric(dend_data$labels$label)]
dend_data$labels$tier <- area_metrics$tier[as.numeric(dend_data$labels$label)]

p_dendrogram <- ggplot(segment(dend_data)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend)) +
  geom_text(data = label(dend_data), 
            aes(x = x, y = y, label = label, color = tier),
            hjust = 1, angle = 90, size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = hc$height[length(hc$height) - optimal_k + 2], 
             linetype = "dashed", color = "red", size = 1) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
  labs(
    title = "Hierarchical Clustering: CLUE Areas",
    subtitle = paste("Dendrogram with", optimal_k, "clusters (red line)"),
    x = NULL,
    y = "Distance"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

# Heatmap of cluster characteristics
cluster_means <- area_metrics %>%
  group_by(tier) %>%
  summarise(
    `Mean Lifespan` = mean(mean_lifespan),
    `Success Rate (%)` = mean(success_rate),
    `Competition` = mean(mean_total_comp),
    `Restaurant Size` = mean(mean_seats),

  ) +

#  STREET-LEVEL CLUSTERING 




# Aggregate metrics by street - CREATE UNIQUE ID
street_metrics <- df_analysis %>%
  group_by(street_address, clue_area) %>%
  summarise(
    # Sample size
    n_businesses = n(),
    
    # Historical performance
    mean_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years),
    median_lifespan = median(lifespan_years),
    success_rate = mean(lifespan_group == ">12 yrs") * 100,
    
    # Competition
    mean_same_ind = mean(same_industry_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_other_ind = mean(other_industry_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_competition = mean(competitors_200m, na.rm = TRUE),
    
    # Business characteristics
    mean_seats = mean(num_seats, na.rm = TRUE),
    pct_cafe = mean(industry == "Cafes") * 100,
    pct_outdoor = mean(str_detect(seating_type, "Outdoor"), na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
    
    # Variability
    sd_lifespan = sd(lifespan_years),
    
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  filter(n_businesses >= 4) %>%  # Only streets with sufficient history
  mutate(
    # CREATE UNIQUE ID: street_area combination
    street_id = paste0(street_address, " (", clue_area, ")")
  )



# Prepare clustering features (standardized)
street_features <- street_metrics %>%
  dplyr::select(
    mean_lifespan,
    success_rate,
    mean_competition
  ) %>%
  scale() %>%
  as.data.frame()

# Use unique street_id as row names
rownames(street_features) <- street_metrics$street_id


# Determine optimal clusters




set.seed(42)
street_sil <- sapply(2:6, function(k) {
  km <- kmeans(street_features, centers = k, nstart = 25)
  ss <- silhouette(km$cluster, dist(street_features))
  mean(ss[, 3])
})

optimal_k_street <- which.max(street_sil) + 1
cat("Optimal clusters:", optimal_k_street, "\n\n")

# Perform clustering




set.seed(42)
km_streets <- kmeans(street_features, centers = optimal_k_street, nstart = 50)

street_metrics$cluster <- km_streets$cluster

# Order clusters by performance
street_cluster_perf <- street_metrics %>%
  group_by(cluster) %>%
  summarise(avg_success = mean(success_rate), .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_success)) %>%
  mutate(rank = row_number())

street_metrics <- street_metrics %>%
  left_join(street_cluster_perf %>% dplyr::select(cluster, rank), by = "cluster") %>%
  mutate(cluster_ordered = rank) %>%
  dplyr::select(-rank)

# Assign tier names
street_tier_names <- c("Gold Streets", "Silver Streets", "Bronze Streets", 
                       "Copper Streets", "Avoid Streets")
street_tier_names <- street_tier_names[1:optimal_k_street]

street_metrics <- street_metrics %>%
  mutate(street_tier = street_tier_names[cluster_ordered])


# Street Cluster Profiles




street_cluster_summary <- street_metrics %>%
  group_by(street_tier, cluster_ordered) %>%
  summarise(
    n_streets = n(),
    n_businesses = sum(n_businesses),
    avg_lifespan = round(mean(mean_lifespan), 1),
    avg_success_rate = round(mean(success_rate), 1),
    avg_competition = round(mean(mean_competition), 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(cluster_ordered)

#print(street_cluster_summary)


# Top 10 streets per tier
for (i in 1:optimal_k_street) {
  tier_streets <- street_metrics %>%
    filter(cluster_ordered == i) %>%
    arrange(desc(success_rate)) %>%
    head(10)
  
  cat(street_tier_names[i], "\n")
  cat(strrep("─", 70), "\n")
  cat("Characteristics:\n")
  cat("  Avg lifespan:", round(mean(tier_streets$mean_lifespan), 1), "years\n")
  cat("  Avg success rate:", round(mean(tier_streets$success_rate), 1), "%\n")
  cat("  Avg competition:", round(mean(tier_streets$mean_competition), 0), "\n\n")
  cat("Top 10 streets:\n")
  for (j in 1:min(10, nrow(tier_streets))) {
    cat(sprintf("  %2d. %-50s - %.1f yrs, %.0f%% success\n",
                j, tier_streets$street_id[j],
                tier_streets$mean_lifespan[j], tier_streets$success_rate[j]))
  }
  cat("\n")
}

# LOAD AND PREPARE DATA



df_full <- read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Get completed lifecycles only (bias-free sample)
df_analysis <- df_full %>%
  filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE, start_year_filter == TRUE) %>%  
  group_by(business_id) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # Log transformation for size
    log_seats = log1p(num_seats),
    
    # Success indicator
    success = (lifespan_group == ">12 yrs"),
    
    # Business age categories
    age_category = case_when(
      lifespan_years <= 3 ~ "Early (1-3 yrs)",
      lifespan_years <= 8 ~ "Established (4-8 yrs)",
      lifespan_years <= 12 ~ "Mature (9-12 yrs)",
      TRUE ~ "Veteran (>12 yrs)"
    ),
    age_category = factor(age_category, levels = c("Early (1-3 yrs)", "Established (4-8 yrs)", 
                                                     "Mature (9-12 yrs)", "Veteran (>12 yrs)")),
    
    # Era categories
    era = case_when(
      census_year <= 2008 ~ "Pre-GFC (2002-2008)",
      census_year <= 2015 ~ "Recovery (2009-2015)",
      TRUE ~ "Modern (2016-2023)"
    ),
    
    # Competition levels
    comp_level = ifelse(other_industry_200m > median(other_industry_200m, na.rm=TRUE), 
                       "High Competition", "Low Competition"),
    
    # Size levels
    size_level = ifelse(num_seats > median(num_seats, na.rm=TRUE), 
                       "Large (>median)", "Small (≤median)")
  )


# Standardize features function
standardize_features <- function(df) {
  df %>%
    mutate(
      same_ind_std = scale(same_industry_200m)[,1],
      other_ind_std = scale(other_industry_200m)[,1],
      log_seats_std = scale(log_seats)[,1],
      foottraffic_std = scale(avg_daily_foottraffic)[,1]
    )
}

df_std <- standardize_features(df_analysis)

# Load street clustering and add street quality indicators to main dataset
street_clusters <- read_csv("clustering_streets.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

df_std <- df_std %>%
  left_join(street_clusters %>% select(street_address, street_tier), 
            by = "street_address") %>%
  mutate(
    # Create best/worst street indicators
    on_best_street = as.numeric(street_tier %in% c("Gold Streets", "Silver Streets")),
    on_worst_street = as.numeric(street_tier %in% c("Copper Streets", "Avoid Streets"))
  )

# Create subset with valid street data for street-specific analyses
df_streets <- df_std %>%
  filter(!is.na(street_tier))


# ANALYSIS 1: GOOD VS POOR STREETS




# Define good vs poor streets (already have street_tier from earlier merge)
df_good_poor <- df_streets %>%
  mutate(
    street_quality = case_when(
      street_tier %in% c("Gold Streets") ~ "Prime Streets",
      street_tier %in% c("Bronze Streets", "Silver Streets") ~ "Poor Streets",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(!is.na(street_quality))



# Function to create comparison plots
create_street_comparison <- function(data, x_var, x_label, title_prefix) {
  
  # Calculate correlations by street quality
  cor_prime <- cor(data %>% filter(street_quality == "Prime Streets") %>% pull({{x_var}}),
                   data %>% filter(street_quality == "Prime Streets") %>% pull(lifespan_years),
                   use = "complete.obs")
  
  cor_poor <- cor(data %>% filter(street_quality == "Poor Streets") %>% pull({{x_var}}),
                  data %>% filter(street_quality == "Poor Streets") %>% pull(lifespan_years),
                  use = "complete.obs")
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x_var}}, y = lifespan_years, color = street_quality)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 0.8) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, size = 1.2) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("Prime Streets" = "#27ae60", "Poor Streets" = "#e74c3c")) +
    annotate("text", x = -Inf, y = Inf, 
             label = paste0("Prime: r=", round(cor_prime, 3), "\nPoor: r=", round(cor_poor, 3)),
             hjust = -0.1, vjust = 1.2, size = 3, fontface = "bold") +
    labs(title = paste(title_prefix, "by Street Quality"),
         x = x_label, y = "Lifespan (years)",
         color = "Street Quality") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom",
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))
}

p1_streets <- create_street_comparison(df_good_poor, same_ind_std, 
                                       "Same-Industry Competition", "A. Same-Industry")
p2_streets <- create_street_comparison(df_good_poor, other_ind_std, 
                                       "Other-Industry Competition", "B. Other-Industry")
p3_streets <- create_street_comparison(df_good_poor, log_seats_std, 
                                       "log(Seats)", "C. Restaurant Size")
p4_streets <- create_street_comparison(df_good_poor %>% filter(!is.na(foottraffic_std)), 
                                       foottraffic_std, "Pedestrians/day", "D. Foot Traffic")

p_streets_final <- (p1_streets | p2_streets) / (p3_streets | p4_streets) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Feature Effects: Prime vs Poor Streets",
    subtitle = "Do success factors work differently on good vs bad streets?",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5))
  )

ggsave("analysis1_good_vs_poor_streets.png", p_streets_final, 
       width = 14, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")

# Create small multiples for each feature
create_area_plot <- function(data, x_var, x_label, title) {
  
  # Calculate correlations by area
  cors <- data %>%
    group_by(clue_area) %>%
    summarise(
      r = cor({{x_var}}, lifespan_years, use = "complete.obs"),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = {{x_var}}, y = lifespan_years, color = clue_area)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2, size = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, size = 1) +
    facet_wrap(~clue_area, ncol = 2) +
    scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1") +
    labs(title = title, x = x_label, y = "Lifespan (years)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
    theme(legend.position = "none",
          plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
          strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

p1_areas <- create_area_plot(df_areas, same_ind_std, 
                             "Same-Industry Competition", "A. Same-Industry by Area")
p2_areas <- create_area_plot(df_areas, other_ind_std, 
                             "Other-Industry Competition", "B. Other-Industry by Area")
p3_areas <- create_area_plot(df_areas, log_seats_std, 
                             "log(Seats)", "C. Size by Area")
p4_areas <- create_area_plot(df_areas %>% filter(!is.na(foottraffic_std)), 
                             foottraffic_std, "Pedestrians/day", "D. Foot Traffic by Area")

p_areas_final <- (p1_areas | p2_areas) / (p3_areas | p4_areas) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Feature Effects by CLUE Area",
    subtitle = "Different neighborhoods, different rules?",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5))

  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_lifespan, 1)), 
            vjust = -1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Large (>median)" = "#27ae60", 
                                 "Small (≤median)" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "D. Does Size Buffer Competition?",
       x = "Competition Level", y = "Average Lifespan (years)",
       color = "Size") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

p_interact_final <- (p1_interact | p2_interact) / (p3_interact | p4_interact) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Interaction Effects: Do Factors Work Together?",
    subtitle = "Testing if size/location can buffer competition effects",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5))
  )

ggsave("analysis4_interactions.png", p_interact_final, 
       width = 14, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")




# ANALYSIS 5: OPTIMAL RANGE ANALYSIS




# Function to create decile analysis
create_decile_plot <- function(data, var, var_label, title) {
  data %>%
    filter(!is.na({{var}})) %>%
    mutate(decile = ntile({{var}}, 10)) %>%
    group_by(decile) %>%
    summarise(
      n = n(),
      avg_value = mean({{var}}, na.rm = TRUE),
      avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
      success_rate = mean(success, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = decile, y = avg_lifespan)) +
    geom_line(color = "#3498db", size = 1.5) +
    geom_point(size = 3, color = "#3498db") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean(data$lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE), 
               linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) +
    labs(title = title,
         x = paste(var_label, "Decile (1=lowest, 10=highest)"),
         y = "Average Lifespan (years)") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))
}

p1_optimal <- create_decile_plot(df_std, num_seats, "Restaurant Size", 
                                 "A. Size Sweet Spot (Inverted-U?)")
p2_optimal <- create_decile_plot(df_std, other_industry_200m, "Other-Industry Competition", 
                                 "B. Competition Effect (Linear Decline?)")
p3_optimal <- create_decile_plot(df_std, same_industry_200m, "Same-Industry Competition", 
                                 "C. Same-Industry Effect")
p4_optimal <- create_decile_plot(df_std %>% filter(!is.na(avg_daily_foottraffic)), 
                                 avg_daily_foottraffic, "Foot Traffic", 
                                 "D. Foot Traffic Effect")

p_optimal_final <- (p1_optimal | p2_optimal) / (p3_optimal | p4_optimal) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Optimal Range Analysis: Finding Sweet Spots",
    subtitle = "Red line = overall average | Looking for non-linear patterns",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5))
  )

ggsave("analysis5_optimal_ranges.png", p_optimal_final, 
       width = 14, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
```

From (Figure \@ref(fig:q19) ), we compare 2,019 businesses that failed within 3 years against 624 businesses achieving >12 year success. The industry composition shows minimal difference—successful establishments are slightly more likely to be cafes (81.6%) versus restaurants compared to failures (74.8%). CBD concentration is virtually identical between groups (63.0% vs 62.7%), challenging assumptions about location primacy.

The most dramatic divergence appears in competitive environment. Successful businesses face less than half the same-industry competition of failures (30.2 vs 64.1 competitors within 200m), and one-third the other-industry competition (11 vs 35). Successful establishments also operate at larger scale, averaging 63.8 seats versus 52.1 for early failures—a 22% size premium.

Competition emerges as the dominant differentiator between success and failure, with a threshold effect around 30-35 same-industry competitors. The similar CBD presence between groups (63%) confirms that being in high-traffic areas alone doesn't ensure success—what matters is the competitive density within those areas. The larger size of successful businesses likely reflects both cause and effect: operators with capital and confidence choose less saturated locations and build larger venues, which in turn provides operational advantages (economies of scale, menu diversity, event capacity) that enhance survival probability.

The 50% reduction in competition for successful businesses suggests they either: (1) strategically selected less saturated micro-locations from inception, (2) benefited from competitor attrition over time, creating breathing room, or (3) established strong positions that deterred new entrants. The 22% size advantage indicates successful operators invest more upfront, suggesting experience and capital—not just location—drive outcomes. The negligible difference in CBD presence reveals that market selection (Carlton vs Southbank vs CBD) matters less than tactical positioning within chosen markets.




#### EDA Summary: Integrated Findings

The exploratory analysis reveals a market shaped by structural forces and geographic dynamics:

Market maturity indicators: The restaurant sector's 5:1 scale advantage reflects higher barriers to entry, but 2018 peak signals saturation. Pre-COVID decline combined with forced downsizing (80→65 seats) indicates transition from growth to optimization phase. Takeaways' continued expansion suggests their niche remains underpenetrated.

Survival paradox: Despite lower barriers to entry, takeaways show higher proportional early-stage failure (45% vs 35%). This suggests ease of entry attracts undercapitalized operators, while restaurant barriers pre-filter for serious players. However, restaurants achieving 5+ year survival demonstrate superior longevity potential.

COVID resilience divergence: Takeaways' rapid recovery versus restaurants' prolonged struggles validates format diversification as risk mitigation. Our client's full-service model should consider takeaway capabilities as defensive strategy.


Critical two-year cliff: Universal 35-45% mortality in years 1-2 transcends industry and geography, suggesting systemic challenges requiring targeted early-stage strategies rather than location selection alone.

These patterns inform our subsequent modeling by highlighting non-linear relationships between scale, competition, and survival requiring sophisticated analytical approaches beyond simple correlation analysis.






### Clustering Analysis

We use clustering on areas and streets—combining longevity, success rate, competition, size, and variability—to uncover natural tiers of location quality. The patterns show a two-stage geography: area-level fundamentals drive survival, while street-level clusters refine choices within those high-quality areas.

( (Figure \@ref(fig:q20) )) integrates competition, lifespan, and business volume by area. Melbourne CBD stands alone as Tier 2 with extreme competition (~125) and massive scale (1500+ businesses), achieving moderate lifespan (5.7 years). Tier 1 areas (red) span a wide competition range (15-50 competitors) while maintaining superior lifespans (5.9-6.5 years). Notably, Tier 3 areas (green) - Kensington and Docklands - show the lowest lifespans (5.2-5.4 years) despite having similar or even lower competition than some Tier 1 areas.

The revised clustering confirms that competition density poorly predicts area performance. East Melbourne (Tier 1) thrives with minimal competition (~15), while Carlton (Tier 1) succeeds with 50+ competitors—over 3x higher. Meanwhile, Docklands (Tier 3) struggles despite moderate competition (~25). The 20-25% lifespan advantage of Tier 1 over Tier 3 areas at similar competition levels definitively proves that inherent location quality—not competitor count—drives area success. Melbourne CBD's unique position suggests it operates under different market dynamics, where extreme volume creates its own ecosystem despite shortened individual lifespans.

( (Figure \@ref(fig:q21) )) quantifies the tier differences through standardized metrics. Tier 1 excels despite having slightly higher competition (21.1) than Tier 3 (18.1), achieving 15.1% success rate versus 7.3%. Tier 1 also features larger restaurants (55.7 seats), longer lifespans (6.3 years), and greater variability. Tier 2 shows extreme competition (123.1)—nearly 6x other tiers—yet maintains moderate success (12.3%). Tier 3 underperforms with the lowest metrics across all dimensions except competition.

This definitively disproves the "low competition = success" hypothesis. Tier 1 areas succeed with MORE competition than struggling Tier 3 areas, achieving double the success rate (15.1% vs 7.3%). The differentiator must be fundamental market quality—Tier 1 locations can support more competitors because they have superior customer bases, accessibility, or complementary businesses that create larger addressable markets.

( (Figure \@ref(fig:q22) ))  indicates nuanced patterns at street level. While many Gold tier streets (yellow) cluster in the low-competition zone (<50 competitors), a striking outlier shows a large Gold street succeeding with 60+ competitors and substantial business volume. More revealing is the mixing of Gold and Bronze streets in the low-competition zone—both street types coexist at similar competition levels (<40) yet achieve vastly different outcomes (7.5-12.5 vs 0-7average lifespan).

Competition fails to fully explain street performance. The presence of successful Gold streets at higher competition levels, combined with Bronze street failures despite minimal competition, indicates critical unmeasured factors drive success. These likely include foot traffic patterns, anchor tenants, street accessibility, parking availability, or proximity to complementary businesses. The large Gold street outlier suggests that exceptional locations can sustain higher density when fundamental attractiveness justifies it—similar to our area-level finding where quality trumps competition





#### Clustering Analysis Summary 

The clustering analysis reveals that Melbourne's restaurant geography operates on multiple, interacting levels:
Location quality trumps competition: The most striking finding is that Tier 1 areas actually have slightly MORE competition (21.1 competitors) than Tier 3 areas (18.1), yet achieve double the success rate (15.1% vs 7.3% in the bias-corrected sample). This definitively proves that competition density is not the primary driver of restaurant success. Instead, inherent area characteristics—likely including residential density, income levels, foot traffic patterns, and complementary retail—create the performance differential.

Competition tolerance varies by quality: Tier 1 areas demonstrate remarkable flexibility, thriving across a wide competition range (15-50 competitors). East Melbourne succeeds with minimal competition while Carlton prospers with 3x higher density. This variability within Tier 1 suggests high-quality locations can adapt to different competitive intensities, while Tier 3 areas fail uniformly despite low competition.

Scale effects persist: The difference in average restaurant size across tiers (55.7 vs 48.2 seats) remains substantial even after bias correction. Areas that attract operators willing to invest in 15% larger formats become successful, indicating location selection and operator quality are interlinked—professional operators recognize and invest in quality locations.

CBD operates as distinct market: Melbourne CBD's extreme competition (123.1)—6x other areas—represents a fundamentally different ecosystem. Maintaining Tier 2 status (12.3% success) despite this density suggests unique demand drivers (tourists, office workers, events) create a larger addressable market with different survival dynamics than neighborhood-based locations.

Hierarchical market structure: The disconnect between area and street patterns reveals multi-scale effects. Areas show quality-driven performance (Tier 1 succeeds despite higher competition), while individual streets show competition sensitivity (Gold and Bronze streets intermingle at low competition but diverge in outcomes). This implies a two-stage selection process—first identify high-quality areas, then navigate street-level competition within them.

Hidden factors dominate: The mixing of Gold and Bronze streets at identical low competition levels (<30 competitors) indicates critical unmeasured variables drive success. These likely include micro-location factors (corner visibility, parking, transit access), anchor tenant effects, or temporal patterns (lunch vs dinner trade) that our competition metrics fail to capture.

These geographic patterns, robust to bias correction, confirm that location fundamentals—not competition levels—drive restaurant survival. The next phase examines whether statistical modeling can quantify these quality factors and their relative importance in predicting success. whether statistical modeling can quantify these inherent location quality factors and their relative importance.


###  Modelling and Determinants of Survival


Following exploratory and clustering analyses, predictive modelling was conducted to quantify how competition, exposure, and business characteristics jointly shape restaurant lifespan. Two complementary approaches were employed:

Random Forest (RF) — a non-linear ensemble method capturing complex, interactive effects (e.g., diminishing returns from foot traffic or saturation thresholds in competition).

Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) — a linear benchmark used to interpret coefficient direction and statistical significance, providing transparency and inference that RF lacks.

This dual-method design combines predictive accuracy with interpretability. The RF identifies which features truly drive survival, while OLS clarifies how they influence it. Together, they form a hybrid evidence base that balances data-driven power with economic reasoning.

```{r}
# Load data
df_shiny <- read_csv("df_clean_200m_shinny.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Select BOTH filter columns needed for merging
filter_info <- df_full %>%
  select(business_id, start_year_filter, complete_lifespan) %>%
```

```{r include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(ranger)      
library(patchwork)
library(scales)







# STEP 1: LOAD AND PREPARE DATA


# Load modeling data
df_model <- read_csv("df_clean_200m_shinny.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)%>%

dplyr:: filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE, start_year_filter == TRUE)



# Remove business_id (not a predictor)
df_features <- df_model %>%
  dplyr::select(-business_id,-on_best_street,-on_worst_street, start_year_filter)

# Check for missing values
na_summary <- colSums(is.na(df_features))
if (sum(na_summary) > 0) {
  cat("⚠ WARNING: Missing values detected:\n")
  print(na_summary[na_summary > 0])
  cat("\nRemoving rows with missing values...\n")
  df_features <- na.omit(df_features)
}




# STEP 2: TRAIN/TEST SPLIT (80/20)




set.seed(42)
train_index <- createDataPartition(
  df_features$lifespan_numeric, 
  p = 0.80,           # 80% training
  list = FALSE,
  times = 1
)

df_train <- df_features[train_index, ]
df_test <- df_features[-train_index, ]



# STEP 3: FEATURE STANDARDIZATION (FOR COMPARISON)


# Identify numeric features (exclude target)
numeric_features <- df_train %>%
  dplyr::select(-lifespan_numeric) %>%
  dplyr::select(where(is.numeric)) %>%
  names()



# Calculate standardization parameters from TRAINING set only
preproc_params <- preProcess(
  df_train[, numeric_features], 
  method = c("center", "scale")
)

# Apply to both train and test
df_train_scaled <- df_train
df_train_scaled[, numeric_features] <- predict(
  preproc_params, 
  df_train[, numeric_features]
)

df_test_scaled <- df_test
df_test_scaled[, numeric_features] <- predict(
  preproc_params, 
  df_test[, numeric_features]
)


# STEP 4: CROSS-VALIDATION SETUP


# 5-fold CV with consistent folds
set.seed(42)
cv_folds <- createFolds(
  df_train$lifespan_numeric, 
  k = 5, 
  returnTrain = TRUE
)

cv_control <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5,
  verboseIter = TRUE,
  savePredictions = "final",
  index = cv_folds,
  allowParallel = TRUE  # Enable parallel processing if available
)


# STEP 5: HYPERPARAMETER TUNING GRID


# Define tuning grid
# For ranger (faster implementation)
n_features <- ncol(df_train) - 1  # Exclude target

tune_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry = c(3, 5, 7, 9, 11),                          # Features per split
  splitrule = c("variance", "extratrees"),           # Splitting rule
  min.node.size = c(5, 10, 20, 30)                   # Min samples per leaf
)


# STEP 6: TRAIN MODELS (NON-STANDARDIZED VS STANDARDIZED)

# MODEL 1: Non-Standardized (Standard for Random Forest)




set.seed(42)
start_time_1 <- Sys.time()

rf_model_raw <- train(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = df_train,
  method = "ranger",
  trControl = cv_control,
  tuneGrid = tune_grid,
  num.trees = 500,
  importance = "impurity",
  num.threads = 4  
)

elapsed_1 <- round(difftime(Sys.time(), start_time_1, units = "mins"), 1)


#print(rf_model_raw$bestTune)

#print(rf_model_raw$results %>% 
#        filter(
 #         mtry == rf_model_raw$bestTune$mtry,
  #        splitrule == rf_model_raw$bestTune$splitrule,
   #       min.node.size == rf_model_raw$bestTune$min.node.size
    #    ) %>%
     #   dplyr::select(RMSE, Rsquared, MAE))


# MODEL 2: Standardized Features (for comparison)



set.seed(42)
start_time_2 <- Sys.time()

rf_model_scaled <- train(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = df_train_scaled,
  method = "ranger",
  trControl = cv_control,
  tuneGrid = tune_grid,
  num.trees = 500,
  importance = "impurity",
  num.threads = 4
)

elapsed_2 <- round(difftime(Sys.time(), start_time_2, units = "mins"), 1)


#print(rf_model_scaled$bestTune)

#print(rf_model_scaled$results %>% 
#        filter(
#          mtry == rf_model_scaled$bestTune$mtry,
#          splitrule == rf_model_scaled$bestTune$splitrule,
#          min.node.size == rf_model_scaled$bestTune$min.node.size
#        ) %>%
#        dplyr::select(RMSE, Rsquared, MAE))


# STEP 7: TEST SET EVALUATION



# Predictions on test set
pred_raw <- predict(rf_model_raw, df_test)
pred_scaled <- predict(rf_model_scaled, df_test_scaled)

# Calculate test metrics
test_metrics <- tibble(
  Model = c("Non-Standardized (RF Standard)", "Standardized (Comparison)"),
  
  `Test RMSE` = c(
    RMSE(pred_raw, df_test$lifespan_numeric),
    RMSE(pred_scaled, df_test$lifespan_numeric)
  ),
  
  `Test MAE` = c(
    MAE(pred_raw, df_test$lifespan_numeric),
    MAE(pred_scaled, df_test$lifespan_numeric)
  ),
  
  `Test R2` = c(
    R2(pred_raw, df_test$lifespan_numeric),
    R2(pred_scaled, df_test$lifespan_numeric)
  ),
  
  `CV RMSE` = c(
    min(rf_model_raw$results$RMSE),
    min(rf_model_scaled$results$RMSE)
  ),
  
  `CV R2` = c(
    max(rf_model_raw$results$Rsquared),
    max(rf_model_scaled$results$Rsquared)
  )
) %>%
  mutate(
    `Overfit Gap (CV-Test R2)` = `CV R2` - `Test R2`,
    `RMSE Diff (CV-Test)` = `CV RMSE` - `Test RMSE`
  )


#print(test_metrics, width = Inf)

# Select best model
best_model <- if (test_metrics$`Test R2`[1] >= test_metrics$`Test R2`[2]) {
  cat("\n✓ WINNER: Non-Standardized model (as expected for Random Forest)\n")
  rf_model_raw
} else {
  cat("\n✓ WINNER: Standardized model (unexpected!)\n")
  rf_model_scaled
}


# STEP 8: FEATURE IMPORTANCE ANALYSIS
```

```{r  include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)

# Step 1: First add foot traffic to shiny dataset
df_shiny <- read_csv("df_clean_200m_shinny.csv")
df_ultra <- read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv")

# Extract foot traffic (first row per business due to time series)
foot_traffic_data <- df_ultra %>%
  group_by(business_id) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(business_id, avg_daily_foottraffic)

# Add foot traffic to shiny
df_shiny_enhanced <- df_shiny %>%
  left_join(foot_traffic_data, by = "business_id")

# Save enhanced dataset
write_csv(df_shiny_enhanced, "df_clean_200m_with_foottraffic.csv")



# Step 2: Create modeling dataset with filters
df_model <- df_shiny_enhanced %>%
  filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE,           # Only closed businesses
         start_year_filter == TRUE,           # Known start date
         !is.na(avg_daily_foottraffic)) %>%  # Has foot traffic
  select(-on_best_street,                     # Remove street indicators
         -on_worst_street, 
         -business_id,                        # REMOVE business ID - critical!
         -start_year_filter,                  # Remove filter columns
         -complete_lifespan)          # REMOVE street indicators


# Step 3: Split data (80/20)
set.seed(42)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(df_model$lifespan_numeric, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- df_model[trainIndex, ]
test_data <- df_model[-trainIndex, ]

# Step 4: Identify numeric features to standardize
numeric_features <- c("same_ind", "other_ind", "log_seats", "avg_daily_foottraffic", 
                     "property_competition")

# Standardize ONLY numeric features
preProcValues <- preProcess(train_data[, numeric_features], method = c("center", "scale"))
train_data_std <- train_data
test_data_std <- test_data

train_data_std[, numeric_features] <- predict(preProcValues, train_data[, numeric_features])
test_data_std[, numeric_features] <- predict(preProcValues, test_data[, numeric_features])

# Step 5: Parameter tuning with CV
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5,
  verboseIter = TRUE
)

# Calculate appropriate mtry values
n_features <- ncol(train_data_std) - 1
mtry_values <- c(floor(sqrt(n_features)), floor(n_features/3), floor(n_features/2))
mtry_values <- unique(mtry_values[mtry_values > 0])


rf_tune <- train(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = train_data_std,
  method = "rf",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = mtry_values),
  ntree = 300
)

# Step 6: Train final model with best parameters
final_rf <- randomForest(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = train_data_std,
  mtry = rf_tune$bestTune$mtry,
  ntree = 500,
  nodesize = 10,
  importance = TRUE
)

# Step 7: Evaluate performance
# Training
train_pred <- predict(final_rf, train_data_std)
train_rmse <- sqrt(mean((train_pred - train_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2))
train_r2 <- cor(train_pred, train_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2

# Test
test_pred <- predict(final_rf, test_data_std)
test_rmse <- sqrt(mean((test_pred - test_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2))
test_r2 <- cor(test_pred, test_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2



# Step 8: Feature importance
importance_df <- data.frame(
  feature = rownames(final_rf$importance),
  importance = final_rf$importance[, "%IncMSE"]
) %>%
  arrange(desc(importance)) %>%
  mutate(
    feature_clean = case_when(
      feature == "avg_daily_foottraffic" ~ "Foot Traffic",
      feature == "same_ind" ~ "Same-Industry Competition", 
      feature == "other_ind" ~ "Other-Industry Competition",
      feature == "log_seats" ~ "Restaurant Size (log)",
      feature == "property_competition" ~ "Property Competition",
      feature == "industry_cafe" ~ "Cafe Business",
      TRUE ~ str_replace_all(feature, "_", " ") %>% str_to_title()
    )
  )

# Plot importance

p_importance <- ggplot(importance_df %>% head(15), 
                      aes(x = reorder(feature_clean, importance), y = importance)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3498db", alpha = 0.8) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(
       x = NULL, y = "Importance (%IncMSE)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

#print(p_importance)

# Step 9: Check foot traffic's importance
foot_rank <- which(importance_df$feature == "avg_daily_foottraffic")
```

```{r R2, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, results = 'show'}
library(dplyr)
library(caret)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

#   extract best CV row from caret model 
best_cv_row <- function(model) {
  # Get the best row based on CV results
  model$results %>%
    filter(mtry == model$bestTune$mtry) %>%
    select(RMSE, Rsquared, MAE)
}

#  Helper: calculate test metrics 
test_metrics <- function(predictions, actual) {
  tibble(
    `Test RMSE` = sqrt(mean((predictions - actual)^2)),
    `Test R2`   = cor(predictions, actual)^2,
    `Test MAE`  = mean(abs(predictions - actual))
  )
}

#  Build comparison table for your RF model 

# Extract CV metrics from rf_tune
cv_metrics <- best_cv_row(rf_tune)

# Calculate test metrics (using already computed predictions)
test_metrics_vals <- test_metrics(test_pred, test_data_std$lifespan_numeric)

# Create full comparison table
tbl_models <- bind_rows(
  tibble(Model = "RF with Foot Traffic") %>%
    bind_cols(
      cv_metrics %>% 
        rename(`CV RMSE` = RMSE, `CV R2` = Rsquared, `CV MAE` = MAE),
      test_metrics_vals
    )
) %>%
  mutate(
    `Overfit Gap (R2)` = `CV R2` - `Test R2`,
    `RMSE Diff` = `Test RMSE` - `CV RMSE`  # Positive = worse on test
  ) %>%
  # Round for display
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 3)))

#  Add training metrics for comparison
train_metrics <- tibble(
  `Train RMSE` = sqrt(mean((train_pred - train_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2)),
  `Train R2` = cor(train_pred, train_data_std$lifespan_numeric)^2,
  `Train MAE` = mean(abs(train_pred - train_data_std$lifespan_numeric))
) %>%
  mutate(across(everything(), ~round(.x, 3)))

# Combine into comprehensive table
tbl_full <- tbl_models %>%
```

</div>




As shown on the table \@ref(tab:R2),two RF models were developed:

* Baseline model: all completed restaurants (n = 3,200).

* Enhanced model: subset including foot-traffic data (n = 2,450).

Despite the smaller sample, incorporating foot-traffic improved accuracy substantially (R²: 0.147 → 0.273; RMSE: 4.19 → 3.97 years, Figure 12). Overfit checks confirmed that the enhanced model generalised well.


Pedestrian activity adds measurable spatial context to survival prediction, reflecting the quality and vitality of trading environments beyond competition and area labels. Although foot-traffic data are biased toward central Melbourne, this bias aligns with the client’s target geography, making the model both representative and actionable.


Competition alone cannot explain performance variance among inner-city venues. Foot traffic captures ambient demand — the real-time potential customer base. By integrating this measure, the model transitions from describing where competition is low to explaining where opportunity endure


```{r q23, fig.align = "center",fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = " Feature Importance - Full Model with Foot Traffic"}
print(p_importance)
```


Feature ranking ( (Figure \@ref(fig:q23) )) confirms a consistent hierarchy across all model runs. Other-Industry Competition and Same-Industry Competition dominate predictive influence, jointly accounting for the majority of model variance. Foot Traffic emerges as the third most critical variable, followed by CBD location, Restaurant Size (log seats), and Business Model (Café vs Restaurant).


Competition variables dominate, but exposure and capacity-related features provide critical secondary effects. Foot traffic’s moderate importance confirms its stabilising power, while “Restaurant vs Takeaway” highlights structural business fragility in low-barrier segments.
Area dummy variables, despite visual prominence in earlier clustering, contribute little unique explanatory power after controlling for quantitative competition and exposure metrics — indicating that location fundamentals are better represented by measurable features (competition, traffic, scale) than categorical suburb labels.


The model effectively deconstructs “location quality” into its operative components. Once competition and footfall intensity are directly measured, the area name itself ceases to add predictive value — a strong validation that the model generalises across geography rather than memorising it.

Competition constrains survival primarily through demand fragmentation. However, high-traffic corridors expand the effective catchment, sustaining adequate patronage despite dense clustering. This interplay between competition and exposure explains why some central zones remain viable even at extreme densities.


```{r diagnostics, include=FALSE}


#  Libraries 
library(tidyverse)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(broom)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(pdp)

#  LOAD AND MERGE DATA 
df_shiny <- read_csv("df_clean_200m_shinny.csv")
df_ultra <- read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv")

# Extract foot traffic (first row per business)
foot_traffic_data <- df_ultra %>%
  group_by(business_id) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(business_id, avg_daily_foottraffic)

# Merge foot traffic into shiny
df_enhanced <- df_shiny %>%
  left_join(foot_traffic_data, by = "business_id")



#  STEP 2: PREPARE MODELING DATASET 
df_model <- df_enhanced %>%
  # Apply filters
  filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE,
         start_year_filter == TRUE,
         !is.na(avg_daily_foottraffic)) %>%
  # Remove ID and unwanted columns
  select(-business_id, 
         -on_best_street, 
         -on_worst_street,
         -start_year_filter,
         -complete_lifespan)

# Remove any remaining NAs
df_model <- na.omit(df_model)


#  TRAIN/TEST SPLIT 
set.seed(42)
trainIndex <- createDataPartition(df_model$lifespan_numeric, p = 0.8, list = FALSE)
train_data <- df_model[trainIndex, ]
test_data <- df_model[-trainIndex, ]



#   STANDARDIZE NUMERIC FEATURES 
numeric_features <- c("same_ind", "other_ind", "log_seats", "avg_daily_foottraffic", 
                     "property_competition")

# Standardization parameters from training set
preProcValues <- preProcess(train_data[, numeric_features], 
                           method = c("center", "scale"))

# Create standardized datasets
train_data_std <- train_data
test_data_std <- test_data
train_data_std[, numeric_features] <- predict(preProcValues, train_data[, numeric_features])
test_data_std[, numeric_features] <- predict(preProcValues, test_data[, numeric_features])

#  TRAIN RANDOM FOREST 
set.seed(42)

# CV setup for tuning
ctrl <- trainControl(
  method = "cv",
  number = 5,
  verboseIter = FALSE
)

# Tune mtry
n_features <- ncol(train_data_std) - 1
mtry_values <- c(floor(sqrt(n_features)), 
                 floor(n_features/3), 
                 floor(n_features/2))

rf_tune <- train(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = train_data_std,
  method = "rf",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = mtry_values),
  ntree = 300
)

# Final model with best parameters
final_rf <- randomForest(
  lifespan_numeric ~ .,
  data = train_data_std,
  mtry = rf_tune$bestTune$mtry,
  ntree = 500,
  nodesize = 10,
  importance = TRUE
)

#   EXTRACT IMPORTANCE AND RUN OLS 
# RF importance
importance_df <- data.frame(
  Feature = rownames(final_rf$importance),
  Overall = final_rf$importance[, "%IncMSE"]
) %>%
  arrange(desc(Overall)) %>%
  mutate(
    Feature_Clean = case_when(
      Feature == "same_ind" ~ "Same-Industry Competition (200m)",
      Feature == "other_ind" ~ "Other-Industry Competition (200m)",
      Feature == "log_seats" ~ "Restaurant Size (log seats)",
      Feature == "avg_daily_foottraffic" ~ "Daily Foot Traffic",
      Feature == "property_competition" ~ "Property-Level Competition",
      Feature == "industry_cafe" ~ "Cafe Business Model",
      Feature == "mixed_seating" ~ "Mixed Seating Type",
      Feature == "outdoor_seating" ~ "Outdoor Seating",
      str_starts(Feature, "clue_") ~ str_replace_all(str_to_title(str_remove(Feature, "clue_")), "_", " "),
      TRUE ~ str_to_title(str_replace_all(Feature, "_", " "))
    )
  )

# OLS for signs and significance (use unstandardized data)
lm_model <- lm(lifespan_numeric ~ ., data = train_data)

# Extract coefficients
tidy_lm <- broom::tidy(lm_model) %>%
  filter(term != "(Intercept)") %>%
  mutate(
    # Clean term names to match RF features
    base_feature = case_when(
      term == "industry_cafe" ~ "industry_cafe",
      term == "mixed_seating" ~ "mixed_seating", 
      term == "outdoor_seating" ~ "outdoor_seating",
      TRUE ~ term
    ),
    direction = case_when(
      estimate > 0 ~ "positive",
      estimate < 0 ~ "negative",
      TRUE ~ "unknown"
    ),
    significance = case_when(
      p.value < 0.001 ~ "***",
      p.value < 0.01 ~ "**",
      p.value < 0.05 ~ "*",
      TRUE ~ ""
    )
  )

# Map RF features to OLS results
feature_mapping <- importance_df %>%
  left_join(
    tidy_lm %>% 
      select(base_feature, direction, significance, p.value),
    by = c("Feature" = "base_feature")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    direction = coalesce(direction, "unknown"),
    significance = coalesce(significance, "")
  )

# ---- STEP 7: CREATE FEATURE IMPORTANCE PLOT ----
p_importance1 <- feature_mapping %>%
  slice_max(Overall, n = 15) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(Feature_Clean, Overall), y = Overall, fill = direction)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.9) +
  coord_flip() +
  # Add significance stars
  geom_text(aes(label = significance), 
            hjust = -0.2, 
            size = 5, 
            fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Direction (from OLS)",
    values = c(
      "negative" = "#d9534f",
      "positive" = "#5cb85c", 
      "unknown" = "#6c757d"
    ),
    drop = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = "Importance Score (%IncMSE)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray40"),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))



# ---- STEP 8: CREATE PDP PLOTS ----
# Generate PDPs
pdp_same <- pdp::partial(final_rf, pred.var = "same_ind", train = train_data_std, plot = FALSE)
pdp_other <- pdp::partial(final_rf, pred.var = "other_ind", train = train_data_std, plot = FALSE)
pdp_size <- pdp::partial(final_rf, pred.var = "log_seats", train = train_data_std, plot = FALSE)
pdp_traffic <- pdp::partial(final_rf, pred.var = "avg_daily_foottraffic", train = train_data_std, plot = FALSE)

# Monochrome PDP plots
p_pdp <- (
  ggplot(pdp_same, aes(x = same_ind, y = yhat)) +
    geom_line(size = 0.5, color = "black") +
    labs(title = "Same-Industry Competition", x = "Competitors (200m)", y = "Predicted Lifespan") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
) + (
  ggplot(pdp_other, aes(x = other_ind, y = yhat)) +
    geom_line(size = 0.5, color = "black") +
    labs(title = "Other-Industry Competition", x = "Competitors (200m)", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
) + (
  ggplot(pdp_size, aes(x = log_seats, y = yhat)) +
    geom_line(size = 0.5, color = "black") +
    labs(title = "Restaurant Size", x = "Log(Seats)", y = "Predicted Lifespan") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
) + (
  ggplot(pdp_traffic, aes(x = avg_daily_foottraffic, y = yhat)) +
    geom_line(size = 0.5, color = "black") +
    labs(title = "Foot Traffic", x = "Daily Pedestrians", y = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10)
) +
  plot_layout(nrow = 2) +
  plot_annotation(
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
  )



# ---- STEP 9: SAVE OUTPUTS ----
ggsave("rf_importance_foottraffic.png", p_importance, width = 10, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
ggsave("pdp_plots_foottraffic.png", p_pdp, width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300, bg = "white")




```

```{r q24, fig.align = "center",fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = " Feature Importance (Top 15) OLS"}
print(p_importance1)
```

While Random Forest identifies which features matter, the OLS overlay ( (Figure \@ref(fig:q24) )) quantifies the direction and strength of these effects.

Competition effects: Both same- and other-industry counts are significantly negative (p < 0.001), confirming their consistent harm across all specifications.

* Foot Traffic: Positive and significant (p < 0.001), verifying that exposure materially enhances longevity.

* Restaurant Size: Positive and significant, though the linear model cannot capture the full U-shape observed in RF.

* CBD presence: Modestly positive (p < 0.01), reflecting stable central demand despite competition.

* Restaurant vs Takeaway: Negative and significant, highlighting structural fragility of low-service formats.


Integrating OLS with RF adds interpretive precision: it distinguishes statistically robust drivers from artefacts of non-linear variance. The linear coefficients confirm that all top-tier variables are meaningful, while low-ranked area factors, despite measurable variance, lack statistical reliability.


OLS offers clarity on average effects, but it assumes constant slopes — an unrealistic simplification for urban systems with tipping dynamics. RF complements this by uncovering curvature and thresholds hidden in the residuals. The two methods are thus symbiotic: OLS explains direction, RF explains pattern.





```{r q25, fig.align = "center",fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Feature comparison OLS"}
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)
library(scales)


# LOAD DATA


df_full <- read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv")

df_analysis <- df_full %>%
   filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE, start_year_filter == TRUE)%>%  
  group_by(business_id) %>%
  slice_head(n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()


# STANDARDIZE FEATURES (z-score: mean=0, sd=1)


df_standardized <- df_analysis %>%
  mutate(
    # Standardize competition metrics
    same_industry_std = scale(same_industry_200m)[,1],
    other_industry_std = scale(other_industry_200m)[,1],
    
    # Standardize size (use log transformation THEN standardize)
    log_seats = log1p(num_seats),
    log_seats_std = scale(log_seats)[,1],
    
    # Standardize foot traffic
    foottraffic_std = scale(avg_daily_foottraffic)[,1]
  )

# Check standardization




# Filter for foot traffic analysis
df_traffic_std <- df_standardized %>% filter(!is.na(foottraffic_std))


# CALCULATE CORRELATIONS (same as before - correlation is scale-invariant)


# Add use = "complete.obs" to handle NA values
cor_same <- cor(df_standardized$same_industry_std, df_standardized$lifespan_years, 
                use = "complete.obs")
cor_other <- cor(df_standardized$other_industry_std, df_standardized$lifespan_years, 
                 use = "complete.obs")
cor_size <- cor(df_standardized$log_seats_std, df_standardized$lifespan_years, 
                use = "complete.obs")
cor_traffic <- cor(df_traffic_std$foottraffic_std, df_traffic_std$lifespan_years, 
                   use = "complete.obs")

# Linear models (use na.action to handle missing values)
lm_same <- lm(lifespan_years ~ same_industry_std, 
              data = df_standardized, na.action = na.exclude)
lm_other <- lm(lifespan_years ~ other_industry_std, 
               data = df_standardized, na.action = na.exclude)
lm_size <- lm(lifespan_years ~ log_seats_std, 
              data = df_standardized, na.action = na.exclude)
lm_traffic <- lm(lifespan_years ~ foottraffic_std, 
                 data = df_traffic_std, na.action = na.exclude)




# CREATE STANDARDIZED PLOTS


# Panel A: Same-Industry Competition (Standardized)
p_same <- ggplot(df_standardized, aes(x = same_industry_std, y = lifespan_years)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 1, color = "#3498db") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e74c3c", fill = "#e74c3c", 
              alpha = 0.2, size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "A. Same-Industry Competition",
       subtitle = "Clear negative relationship → Keep in model",
       x = "Competitors (200m)", y = "Lifespan (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#2c3e50"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#27ae60"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, size = 0.8))

# Panel B: Other-Industry Competition (Standardized)
p_other <- ggplot(df_standardized, aes(x = other_industry_std, y = lifespan_years)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 1, color = "#1abc9c") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e74c3c", fill = "#e74c3c", 
              alpha = 0.2, size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "B. Other-Industry Competition",
       subtitle = "Strong negative relationship → Keep in model",
       x = "Competitors (200m)", y = "Lifespan (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#2c3e50"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#27ae60"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, size = 0.8))

# Panel C: Restaurant Size (Log-transformed THEN Standardized)
p_size <- ggplot(df_standardized, aes(x = log_seats_std, y = lifespan_years)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 1, color = "#f39c12") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e74c3c", fill = "#e74c3c", 
              alpha = 0.2, size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "C. Restaurant Size",
       subtitle = "Modest relationship (non-linear) → Keep in model",
       x = "log(Seats)", y = "Lifespan (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#2c3e50"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#f39c12"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, size = 0.8))

# Panel D: Foot Traffic (Standardized)
p_traffic <- ggplot(df_traffic_std, aes(x = foottraffic_std, y = lifespan_years)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 1, color = "#95a5a6") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e74c3c", fill = "#e74c3c", 
              alpha = 0.2, size = 1.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50", size = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "D. Foot Traffic (Pedestrian Count)",
       subtitle = "No meaningful relationship → EXCLUDED from model",
       x = "Pedestrians/day", y = "Lifespan (years)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#2c3e50"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#e74c3c"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "gray80", fill = NA, size = 0.8))


# COMBINE PLOTS


p_final <- (p_same + p_other) / (p_size + p_traffic) +
  plot_annotation(
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12, color = "gray30"),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, color = "gray50", hjust = 0, lineheight = 1.2)
    )
  )


# SAVE PLOT


ggsave("feature_comparison_4panel_STANDARDIZED.png", p_final,
       width = 16, height = 12, dpi = 300, bg = "white")


# SUMMARY STATISTICS


summary_stats <- tibble(
  Feature = c("Same-Industry Competition", "Other-Industry Competition", 
              "Restaurant Size (log)", "Foot Traffic"),
  `Original Mean` = c(
    round(mean(df_standardized$same_industry_200m), 1),
    round(mean(df_standardized$other_industry_200m), 1),
    round(mean(df_standardized$log_seats), 2),
    round(mean(df_standardized$avg_daily_foottraffic, na.rm=TRUE), 0)
  ),
  `Original SD` = c(
    round(sd(df_standardized$same_industry_200m), 1),
    round(sd(df_standardized$other_industry_200m), 1),
    round(sd(df_standardized$log_seats), 2),
    round(sd(df_standardized$avg_daily_foottraffic, na.rm=TRUE), 0)
  ),
  `Std Mean` = c(
    round(mean(df_standardized$same_industry_std), 3),
    round(mean(df_standardized$other_industry_std), 3),
    round(mean(df_standardized$log_seats_std), 3),
    round(mean(df_standardized$foottraffic_std, na.rm=TRUE), 3)
  ),
  `Std SD` = c(
    round(sd(df_standardized$same_industry_std), 3),
    round(sd(df_standardized$other_industry_std), 3),
    round(sd(df_standardized$log_seats_std), 3),
    round(sd(df_standardized$foottraffic_std, na.rm=TRUE), 3)
  ),
  Correlation = c(cor_same, cor_other, cor_size, cor_traffic)
) %>%
  mutate(Correlation = round(Correlation, 3))

#print(summary_stats)


# Display plot
print(p_final)


```

Linear regressions ( (Figure \@ref(fig:q25) )) of standardised features provide a baseline for comparison.

Same- and Other-Industry Competition show clear negative slopes, matching expectations.

Restaurant Size shows a mild positive correlation, while Foot Traffic appears near-flat under a linear specification.

Insight:
At first glance, foot traffic seems inconsequential. However, its later importance within the non-linear RF model indicates that the effect is threshold-driven rather than proportional—only areas surpassing a certain pedestrian density see meaningful gains.

Why this pattern exists:
Linear methods fail to capture saturation or tipping effects inherent in urban systems. Pedestrian influence likely activates only beyond critical mass, where consistent passing flow translates into reliable custom. The RF model’s structure allows such non-linear thresholds to surface.





```{r q26, fig.align = "center",fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Partial Dependence Plots"}

print(p_pdp)
```



Partial Dependence Plots ( (Figure \@ref(fig:q26) ))illustrate marginal effects while holding other features constant, isolating pure influence patterns.


Same-Industry Competition: Lifespan declines sharply with the first few competitors and stabilises as competion increased, confirming a saturation threshold. Markets reach carrying capacity where additional competitors don't further fragment demand—the pie is already fully divided. This explains why CBD businesses survive despite 20+ nearby competitors: beyond a threshold, competition intensity becomes background noise.

Other-Industry Competition: Similar steep decline, with wider range indicating broader crowding sensitivity. Marginal harm diminishes .

Restaurant Size: Exhibits a U-shaped pattern—micro-cafés and large venues outperform mid-scale operators, suggesting both niche and scale strategies can succeed. this indicates that those mid-size venues face the worst of both worlds—high fixed costs without scale benefits.

Foot Traffic: Nearly flat at low pedestrian levels, then climbs steadily beyond mid-range, confirming a non-linear exposure benefit.The relationship is non-compensatory — traffic can't offset poor competition position


The PDP visualises the marginal return curve of each factor, revealing hidden dynamics: competition harm saturates early, while foot traffic benefits accelerate late. This asymmetric response explains why some dense areas remain profitable — high exposure compensates for market crowding.

The model implicitly captures market equilibrium — low-competition areas fail without sufficient demand, while high-competition zones remain viable only if traffic supports them. PDPs thus reconcile the earlier contradiction observed in clustering analysis: competition matters, but only relative to available demand.



#### Section Summary

This modelling phase transforms prior descriptive insights into quantified causal patterns.

Random Forest isolates non-linear, interactive dynamics underpinning survival.

OLS provides statistical validation and interpretive transparency.

PDP visualises true marginal responses beyond linear simplification.

Key findings align tightly with earlier geographic patterns:

* Competition intensity remains the dominant constraint, cutting average lifespan by up to 40% within 200 m of dense clusters.

* Foot traffic operationalises “location quality”, validating its 50% uplift in model explanatory power (R²: 0.27 vs 0.15).

* Restaurant scale shapes resilience through a U-shaped pattern, with small venues (<40 seats) and large-format establishments (>120 seats) outperforming mid-sized operations (50-100 seats), suggesting that clear positioning at either end of the scale spectrum provides competitive advantages.

* Area labels contribute minimal residual value, confirming that measurable spatial features explain survival more effectively than categorical geography.


* The dual-model approach bridges spatial and statistical reasoning. Clustering showed Tier 1 areas succeed despite competition; this section explains why—high exposure and size resilience offset density effects.


































### Interaction Analysis



The previous section established that competition intensity, size, and foot-traffic exposure are the dominant individual determinants of restaurant longevity. However, these factors rarely operate in isolation. This section examines how they interact — whether certain combinations reinforce or mitigate one another — to reveal the deeper structure of survival dynamics in Melbourne’s hospitality market. Figure 17 summarises these interaction effects across four panels, drawing on bias-corrected averages for completed restaurants.

```{r include=FALSE}

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

# Load & prep 
df_full <- readr::read_csv("df_ULTRA_enhanced_with_traffic.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

df_std <- df_full %>%
   filter(complete_lifespan == TRUE, start_year_filter == TRUE) %>%             
  group_by(business_id) %>% slice_head(n = 1) %>% ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    # total competition = same + other
    comp_total = coalesce(same_industry_200m, 0) + coalesce(other_industry_200m, 0),
    # median splits
    comp_level = if_else(
      comp_total > median(comp_total, na.rm = TRUE), "High Competition", "Low Competition",
      missing = NA_character_
    ),
    size_level = if_else(
      num_seats > median(num_seats, na.rm = TRUE), "Large (>median)", "Small (≤median)",
      missing = NA_character_
    )
  )

# enforce 2-level order and drop NA competition rows for any plot
df_std <- df_std %>%
  mutate(
    comp_level = factor(comp_level, levels = c("High Competition", "Low Competition")),
    size_level = factor(size_level, levels = c("Large (>median)", "Small (≤median)"))
  )

df_noNAcomp <- df_std %>% filter(!is.na(comp_level))

#  PANEL A: Competition × Size (unchanged design)
interactionA <- df_noNAcomp %>%
  filter(!is.na(size_level)) %>%
  group_by(comp_level, size_level) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p1_interact <- ggplot(interactionA, aes(x = comp_level, y = size_level, fill = avg_lifespan)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f yrs", avg_lifespan, n)),
            fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e74c3c", mid = "#f39c12", high = "#27ae60",
                       midpoint = mean(df_noNAcomp$lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE)) +
  labs(
       x = "Competition Level", y = "Restaurant Size", fill = "Avg Lifespan") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

#  Choose the two areas for Panels B/C 
area_pair <- c("Carlton", "Docklands")

df_area_pair <- df_noNAcomp %>%
  filter(clue_area %in% area_pair) %>%
  mutate(area_2 = factor(clue_area, levels = area_pair))   # lock order: Carlton, Docklands

#  PANEL B: Competition × Area (2×2, NO NA column) 
interactionB <- df_area_pair %>%
  group_by(comp_level, area_2) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p2_interact <- ggplot(interactionB, aes(x = comp_level, y = area_2, fill = avg_lifespan)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f yrs", avg_lifespan, n)),
            fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e74c3c", mid = "#f39c12", high = "#27ae60",
                       midpoint = mean(df_area_pair$lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE)) +
  labs(
       x = "Competition Level", y = "CLUE Area", fill = "Avg Lifespan") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# PANEL C: Size × Area (2×2) 
interactionC <- df_area_pair %>%
  filter(!is.na(size_level)) %>%
  group_by(size_level, area_2) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p3_interact <- ggplot(interactionC, aes(x = size_level, y = area_2, fill = avg_lifespan)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f yrs", avg_lifespan, n)),
            fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e74c3c", mid = "#f39c12", high = "#27ae60",
                       midpoint = mean(df_area_pair$lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE)) +
  labs(
       x = "Restaurant Size", y = "CLUE Area", fill = "Avg Lifespan") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

#  PANEL D: Does Size Buffer Competition? 
interactionD <- df_noNAcomp %>%
  filter(!is.na(size_level)) %>%
  group_by(comp_level, size_level) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p4_interact <- ggplot(interactionD, aes(x = comp_level, y = avg_lifespan,
                                        color = size_level, group = size_level)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_lifespan, 1)),
            vjust = -1, fontface = "bold", size = 3.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Large (>median)" = "#27ae60", "Small (≤median)" = "#e74c3c")) +
  labs(title = "D. Does Size Buffer Competition?",
       x = "Competition Level", y = "Average Lifespan (years)", color = "Size") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"))

# save
p_interact_final <- (p1_interact | p2_interact) / (p3_interact | p4_interact) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "Interaction Effects: Do Factors Work Together?",
    subtitle = "Panels B/C use Areas. Competition = total competitors within 200m. Rows with missing competition are dropped.",
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, hjust = 0.5))
  )

ggsave("interaction_4panel_AREA_competition_noNA.png",
       p_interact_final, width = 14, height = 10, dpi = 300, bg = "white")


```





Figure \@ref(fig:q27) compares restaurants above and below the median seating size under high- and low-competition conditions. A clear buffering pattern emerges: under high competition, small venues perform poorly (4.5 yrs) whereas larger ones fare moderately better (5.1 yrs). When competition is low, both size groups enjoy longer survival, but large venues again lead (7.2 yrs vs 6.4 yrs).
This indicates that scale offers resilience, likely through operational flexibility and brand visibility that help larger venues sustain profits in denser markets.


```{r q28, fig.align = "center",fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Competition × Area (Carlton vs Docklands)"}


p2_interact
```

From (Figure \@ref(fig:q28), area-specific contrasts highlight spatial heterogeneity in competitive tolerance.
In Docklands, even moderate rivalry sharply reduces survival (2.2 yrs → 5.2 yrs). In Carlton, businesses exhibit greater durability (4.3 yrs → 6.8 yrs), suggesting stronger demand fundamentals and a more stable customer base.
Hence, competition interacts with local market maturity — well-established precincts absorb rivalry better than newly developed areas.

```{r q29, fig.align = "center",fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Size × Area"}


p3_interact 
```



Figure \@ref(fig:q29) examines whether the benefits of scale vary by area. Size advantages are not uniform across locations.
In Carlton, both large and small venues achieve relatively long lifespans (6.4 yrs vs 6.0 yrs), implying balanced demand across scales.
Conversely, in Docklands, smaller operators underperform (4.7 yrs) relative to larger ones (5.5 yrs). This reinforces the notion that larger spaces confer stability where market demand is still forming or volatile, as they can better accommodate diverse offerings and customer volumes.



```{r q30, fig.align = "center",fig.width=6, fig.height=2.5, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE, fig.cap = "Competition × Foot Traffic"}


# Add foot-traffic bucket and total competition in the *EDA frame*
df_std2 <- df_std %>%
  mutate(
    comp_total = coalesce(same_industry_200m, 0) + coalesce(other_industry_200m, 0),
    traffic_level = if_else(
      avg_daily_foottraffic > median(avg_daily_foottraffic, na.rm = TRUE),
      "High Foot Traffic", "Low Foot Traffic",
      missing = NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    comp_level    = factor(comp_level,    levels = c("High Competition", "Low Competition")),
    traffic_level = factor(traffic_level, levels = c("High Foot Traffic", "Low Foot Traffic"))
  )

# Drop rows missing competition or traffic
df_xy <- df_std2 %>% filter(!is.na(comp_level), !is.na(traffic_level))

interactionD2 <- df_xy %>%
  group_by(comp_level, traffic_level) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    avg_lifespan = mean(lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

p4_interact_ft_tile <- ggplot(interactionD2, aes(x = comp_level, y = traffic_level, fill = avg_lifespan)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.1f yrs", avg_lifespan)), fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#e74c3c", mid = "#f39c12", high = "#27ae60",
    midpoint = mean(df_xy$lifespan_years, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Competition Level", y = "Foot Traffic Level", fill = "Avg Lifespan"
  ) +
```
